claims.text: Resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion in high-entropy alloys is governed by dynamic formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline surface layer.
Localized wear stresses induce surface grain refinement or partial amorphization.
The dynamically refined surface layer stabilizes an enhanced passive film.
The refined surface and enhanced passive film have a lower density of active defects.
The ultra-nanocrystalline layer acts as a structural barrier that reduces abrasive material removal.
The refined layer and passive film reduce corrosive attack by lowering the density of active defect sites.
Mechanical wear in a corrosive NaCl environment can induce localized plastic deformation and dynamic grain refinement or amorphization.
An HEA that dynamically refines during wear will have a lower wear rate than a matched coarse-grained or refinement-inhibited baseline.
An HEA that dynamically refines during wear will have a lower corrosion current density than the matched baseline.
Combined tribocorrosion degradation will be significantly lower than degradation caused by either wear or corrosion acting alone.
The prediction applies to HEAs with an intrinsic capacity for stress-induced dynamic grain refinement or amorphization.
The proposed benefit may fail in alloys whose microstructures are too thermally or chemically stable to transform dynamically.
A fine initial microstructure and lower stability against plastic deformation favor dynamic grain refinement during wear.
Alloying elements can be used to stabilize coarse grains and thereby inhibit dynamic refinement.
The refinement-favored group should develop a significantly finer, passivated near-surface layer under tribocorrosion testing.
XPS can characterize both passive-film composition and passive-film defect density in the proposed test.

contradictions.description: The baseline is described as not subjected to deformation cycling, but the controlled comparison also requires both groups to undergo identical simultaneous mechanical abrasion or cyclic loading. A no-cycling baseline cannot simultaneously receive the same wear exposure.

The two groups are required to have the same nominal composition, yet minor alloying and addition of grain-stabilizing elements are proposed as ways to differentiate them; those approaches would ordinarily change nominal composition.

The stated initial material is relatively coarse and at equilibrium, whereas the refinement-favored experimental group is proposed to begin with a fine microstructure. The experiment therefore does not cleanly instantiate the initial state specified for the hypothesis.
